questions.q: According to this lesson, does copying real customer data into a sandbox reduce its sensitivity?
options: Yes, data automatically becomes anonymized the moment it's copied into any sandbox
No -- the data is exactly as sensitive in a sandbox as it is in production; copying it just creates a second place that sensitive data now lives
Yes, but only for Partial Copy sandboxes, not Full sandboxes
Sensitivity only applies to data stored in production, by definition
questions.explain: A customer's SSN or health information doesn't become less sensitive by being copied into a sandbox -- it just now exists in a second location with its own access list and exposure risk.

questions.q: Which two sandbox types directly create the real-data exposure risk this lesson describes?
options: Developer and Developer Pro
Developer and Full
Partial Copy and Full
None -- no sandbox type ever carries real production records
questions.explain: Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes are metadata-only; Partial Copy carries a sampled subset of real records and Full carries all of production's data, which is what creates this specific exposure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say sandboxes are sometimes the LEAST protected place an organization's sensitive data exists?
options: Because sandboxes technically cannot have any access controls applied to them
Because Salesforce does not allow any security settings to be configured in a sandbox

Because the "it's just a sandbox" mindset often leads to looser credential sharing, slower-growing scrutiny of access lists, and long gaps between refreshes, even while holding the same real data production has
Because sandboxes are always visible to the public internet by default
questions.explain: Sandboxes are often treated with far less rigor than production precisely because they're seen as lower-stakes, even when they hold the exact same sensitive real data -- the opposite of what that reputation would suggest.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say sandbox data risk and sandbox access control compound each other rather than simply adding up?
options: Because a wide-open access list turns "sensitive data exists in this sandbox" into "sensitive data is actually exposed to people who shouldn't see it" -- not just two separate problems sitting side by side
Because access control and data risk are actually the same exact thing with different names
Because Salesforce automatically doubles the risk score of any sandbox with more than one user
Because compounding only applies to Developer sandboxes, not Partial Copy or Full
questions.explain: A loosely managed access list combined with real sensitive data present is worse than either factor alone -- shrinking either side (fewer people with access, or less sensitive data present) reduces the real risk.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the standard way to reduce sandbox data risk without giving up realistic testing?
options: Deleting all Partial Copy and Full sandboxes permanently
Granting every user access to every sandbox so no one feels excluded
Refusing to ever use Partial Copy or Full sandboxes under any circumstance
Data masking -- transforming real sensitive values into realistic-looking but fake ones once they land in a non-production environment
questions.explain: Data masking is this lesson's named bridge into Lesson 10 -- it preserves realistic data shapes for testing while removing the actual sensitive values that create the exposure risk.
